summary:
FireLert is an interactive web application that turns NASA FIRMS satellite observations into a historical burning activity calendar. Developed by AstraXShip, it focuses on Indonesia and Malaysia, with records spanning 2003–2024.

The project addresses the MODIS and VIIRS harmonization challenge by calibrating observations to an Aqua reference scale, helping users distinguish changes in burning activity from differences between satellite instruments. Users can select countries and dates, compare raw and harmonized records, explore seasonal patterns and unusual periods, and inspect the evidence behind individual weeks. An annual activity map and interactive globe provide geographic context, while downloadable data and shareable views support further investigation.

FireLert matters because inconsistent satellite records can make historical patterns difficult to interpret. By making source observations, calibration results and remaining uncertainty visible, it helps scientists and land managers investigate burning activity more transparently. It supports historical understanding not forecasting or emergency alerts and treats hotspots as detections rather than distinct fires.
details:
What does it do?

FireLert is an interactive web application that helps users explore historical burning activity and ask an important question: Did burning change—or did the satellite instrument change?

NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS instruments detect active fire hotspots at different spatial resolutions, sensitivities and observation schedules. Their raw detection counts cannot be treated as directly equivalent. Joining these records without accounting for instrument differences can make a sensor transition look like a change in burning activity.

FireLert addresses this challenge through a historical burning activity calendar, raw-versus-harmonized comparisons, geographic visualizations and traceable evidence. Our regional focus is Indonesia and Malaysia, with published records covering 2003–2024. Additional country records are available for comparison.

How does it work?

The application uses NASA FIRMS MODIS Terra/Aqua and Suomi-NPP VIIRS observations. For Indonesia and Malaysia, data preparation involved 78 verified annual archives and 5,038,770 cleaned observations.

The processing workflow preserves satellite identities, cleans observations, aggregates counts and calibrates VIIRS activity to a MODIS Aqua reference scale. This expresses converted observations in Aqua-equivalent units, making the historical record easier to compare. Aqua is a common reference—not ground truth.

We separated model development and evaluation into:

  • Training: 2013–2017
  • Validation and model selection: 2018–2019
  • Held-out testing: 2020–2024

Validation selected model B1 for Indonesia and M1 for Malaysia. Their monthly test biases against Aqua were −11.05% and −15.84%, respectively. These results show that calibration error remains; they are not accuracy percentages.

Users can:

  • Select a country and date range.
  • Compare raw and harmonized weekly calendars.
  • Investigate seasonal patterns and unusual historical periods.
  • Open a week to inspect separate sensor counts, transformations and reported calibration bounds.
  • Explore annual activity through a 2D geographic map and an optional interactive 3D globe.
  • Inspect daily records for selected grid cells.
  • Export CSV data, export historical seasonal periods as calendar files, and share supported exploration settings.

The annual map has its own year selector and represents full-year activity, rather than arbitrary date-range totals.

Benefits and intended impact

FireLert is designed to support scientists, land managers and other users investigating historical burning activity. Its intended benefit is to make long-term patterns easier to interpret without overlooking differences between satellite instruments.

Instead of presenting a heatmap alone, FireLert connects a visible pattern to its supporting observations. Users can examine the evidence, check available-day counts and understand how an estimate was produced before drawing conclusions.

The project supports historical investigation and contextual understanding. It is not a live fire detector, forecasting system or emergency alert service.

Tools and technologies

FireLert uses:

  • Python, pandas and NumPy for data preparation, aggregation, calibration and evaluation.
  • React and TypeScript for the interactive web interface.
  • Vite for development and production builds.
  • Three.js for the interactive Earth visualization.
  • HTML Canvas for the annual 2D activity map.
  • Natural Earth geographic data, packaged through world-atlas and processed with TopoJSON tools.
  • GitHub for source management and Vercel for web hosting.

The application serves preprocessed datasets as a static website, allowing users to explore the published record without running the scientific pipeline themselves. No custom sensing hardware was developed.

What makes the project creative?

FireLert’s central idea is to make comparability and evidence part of the user experience. The raw/harmonized switch lets users question whether an apparent change reflects burning activity or instrument differences. Weekly evidence panels connect charts to source observations, while maps connect the temporal record to geographic context.

The result is a connected workflow:

Explore a pattern → compare the signals → inspect the evidence → share the record.

Factors we considered

Scientific transparency guided the design. Hotspots are detections—not distinct fires or burned area. Archive completeness does not establish cloud-free observation coverage, missing observations do not mean zero burning, and national evaluation does not establish local-cell accuracy. Daily geographic detail is limited to selected cells, and reported calibration bounds do not represent total uncertainty.

We also considered accessible controls, readable visualizations, downloadability and reproducibility. Shared links preserve supported exploration settings, but are not immutable dataset snapshots.

FireLert is adapted from the MIT-licensed FIRETRACE foundation, with attribution retained. NASA FIRMS supplies the observations, Natural Earth supplies geographic context, and AI assistance is disclosed in the repository.
